name: LF Edge

stages.name: At-Large
stages.summary: Stage 1: usually early projects the Technical Advisory Council considers important, or potentially important, to edge computing.

stages.name: Growth
stages.summary: Stage 2: projects with a plan to reach the Impact stage, still building their product while they start to support adopters at scale.

stages.name: Impact
stages.summary: Stage 3: self-sustaining projects with ongoing development and long-term support, widely used in production by a broad, established community.

stages.name: Emeritus
stages.summary: Retired projects that LF Edge still lists but no longer counts among its active ones.

summary: The Linux Foundation’s umbrella for edge computing: EdgeX Foundry, Akraino, EVE, Open Horizon and ten more projects for running software near sensors and machines, each at an At-Large, Growth or Impact stage.
intro: LF Edge is part of the non-profit Linux Foundation. The Linux Foundation launched it on January 24, 2019 as an umbrella for edge computing, aiming at an open framework that doesn’t depend on any one kind of hardware, silicon, cloud or operating system. It started with five projects and more than 60 member organisations, including Arm, AT&T, Dell EMC, Huawei, IBM, Intel, Red Hat, Samsung and ZEDEDA. Two projects that already lived at the Linux Foundation moved in: EdgeX Foundry, from Dell, and the Akraino Edge Stack, from AT&T. Samsung seeded a new Home Edge project and ZEDEDA contributed Project EVE, an operating system for edge hardware.

In October 2026 its projects page listed 14 active projects: five at the Impact stage (Akraino, EdgeX Foundry, EVE, Fledge and Open Horizon), three at Growth (EdgeLake, FIDO Device Onboard and State of the Edge) and six At-Large (eKuiper, InfiniEdge AI, InstantX, NanoMQ, Nexoedge and Ocre), plus three in an Emeritus tab (Alvarium, Baetyl and Home Edge). Each project keeps its own technical steering committee; LF Edge’s Technical Advisory Council (TAC) coordinates between them and votes new projects in, and a Governing Board of paying members handles the budget.

For someone choosing a technology, an LF Edge badge says the project’s name and governance sit with the Linux Foundation rather than the company that started it, and that the TAC has looked at it. The stage says more than the badge: Impact means a project the TAC considers self-sustaining and widely used in production, while At-Large is the entry level, which the TAC describes as typically early-stage. Many projects were started by a single company and still lean on it: eKuiper and NanoMQ come from EMQ, which pairs them with its EMQX broker, and EVE from ZEDEDA. The projects target factories, vehicles, shops and telecom sites, so most are a long way from the cloud services elsewhere in this handbook.

sections.title: At-Large to Impact, and Emeritus
sections.intro: Stage definitions and project lists are from the LF Edge projects page in October 2026. Every project, whatever its stage, may attend TAC meetings and contribute.

items.name: At-Large
items.text: Stage 1. Projects the TAC considers important, or potentially important, to the edge ecosystem, typically early-stage, which add capabilities to LF Edge in return for community support. A project is voted in by two-thirds of the TAC, and the Governing Board then approves it: eKuiper, from EMQ, was put to the TAC in April 2021. The other At-Large projects are InfiniEdge AI, InstantX, NanoMQ, Nexoedge and Ocre.

items.name: Growth
items.text: Stage 2. Projects aiming for Impact that have a growth plan and are still building their product while starting to support adopters at scale: EdgeLake, FIDO Device Onboard and State of the Edge.

items.name: Impact
items.text: Stage 3. Self-sustaining projects with ongoing development, maintenance and long-term support, widely used in production with many public use cases. Akraino, EdgeX Foundry, EVE, Fledge and Open Horizon are at this stage; EdgeX Foundry, the oldest, ships long-term support releases such as 4.0, supported until March 2027.

items.name: Emeritus
items.text: Projects LF Edge no longer counts as active but still lists: Alvarium, Baetyl and Home Edge, one of the five projects LF Edge started with.

story: Edge computing projects arrived at the Linux Foundation one at a time. Dell gave its FUSE IoT code, more than a dozen microservices and over 125,000 lines, to start EdgeX Foundry in April 2017, and AT&T contributed the Akraino Edge Stack for telecom edge sites. Each had its own board and membership, and companies such as Intel, Huawei and Arm joined several overlapping efforts at once.

On January 24, 2019 the Linux Foundation pulled them under one umbrella, LF Edge, with five anchor projects and more than 60 founding members. EdgeX Foundry, Akraino and the Open Glossary of Edge Computing moved in; Samsung’s Home Edge and ZEDEDA’s EVE were new. Projects kept their own technical steering committees, while a shared Governing Board and TAC replaced the separate funds.

Later arrivals were mostly small projects from single companies, such as EMQ’s eKuiper, a stream processing engine voted in at the At-Large stage in 2021. By October 2026, LF Edge listed 14 active projects in three stages and three emeritus ones, including Home Edge.

choices.choice: One umbrella instead of separate foundations
choices.why: Members were paying into several edge projects with overlapping goals. A single fund and TAC let projects share events, staff and a lifecycle while keeping their own code and steering committees.

choices.choice: Stages based on use, not just code
choices.why: Impact requires many public production use cases and a broad community, so a badge tells users how far a project has spread, not only that it was accepted.

choices.choice: Independent of hardware, silicon, cloud and operating system
choices.why: Edge sites run on very different machines, from industrial gateways to telecom racks, so LF Edge set out to build a framework that doesn’t tie users to any one vendor’s stack.
